name: Dana Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day at the accounting firm.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I put the florist's till slips in date order, enter the sales, and prepare the simple accounts and tax schedules for a senior to check. I like when a whole week balances to the bank, but being handed a wet bag of receipts just before closing makes me want to go home. I am 58 and have a bachelor's degree in accounting; I am still learning the firm's way of doing returns, not leading anybody. I have never used an AI tool, and I prefer the ledger I can check line by line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI turns out mostly to be hype, I still have the florist's slips and a senior checking my schedules. Maybe the scanner saves a few minutes, but I would still enter the dates carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team to keep the simple checklist before sending the figures upstairs. I would tell the florist that someone still reads the receipts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am on the lower end of pay for this job, with less than a month of expenses saved. My partner Farah's part-time laundry work helps with our rent, and our grown children have their own households; there are few similar accounting jobs nearby, so even a quiet year feels tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep entering the paid florist returns and use the present checklist. I would cancel the extra television package next month and transfer that monthly charge into a cash account, but only while our rent, food and travel are covered by actual pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bills even in a mild AI story. I cannot call a thin account a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help if money ran out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have bills of their own. I would ask for advice before money, and I would not put their wages into my budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cancel the television package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is the one charge I can stop without losing a work journey or a meal. The transfer is small, but it is a real new deposit if the pay arrives.

say: I would keep the **simple checklist** before sending returns upstairs.
I would tell the florist a **person reads** the receipts.
think: My **low pay** and under-one-month reserve make ordinary bills stressful.
Few nearby jobs and Farah's part-time wage limit our **fallback income**.
do: Keep entering **paid florist returns** under the current checklist.
Cancel the **television package** and deposit its charge only after rent, food and work travel are covered.
S0.quote: I cannot call a thin account a retirement plan.
fieldNote: The mild scenario does not erase **baseline financial worry**: low pay, rent and less than one month saved.
Her new cash deposit comes from a **cancelled recurring charge**, conditional on actual pay covering essentials.

steps.text: Keep paid florist returns and current checklist
Cancel television package and deposit charge only after rent food and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and entering numbers are exactly what the card says AI will take first. A robot might later move flower boxes, but my desk work would change now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff union for written notice if our hours are cut and paid time for any required training. I would tell the senior I will not sign a number I cannot trace to a receipt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to cut a large part of my junior hours when the software enters and checks the slips. Farah's laundry shifts will not pay our rent alone, and I have almost no cash cushion; that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would join the staff union and ask it to seek notice and paid training before hours change. I would take the firm's required AI walkthrough only if it is on paid time with a written job requirement, then continue the paid florist files still assigned; if my hours fall in the first year, I would apply to posted accounts-clerk openings only with written pay, hours and a start date covering rent and the bus to work. I would not quit the shifts still offered just because the tool looks fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large wage cut and have little time to absorb it. I can learn a required screen if someone pays me to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI on the florist's file alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have never used it and I would not guess on a client's tax figures. A supervisor must show me the approved tool on paid time first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you commute farther?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written wage after the bus fare still covers rent and food. There are few firms nearby, and a long journey could eat a small pay rise.

say: I would ask the **staff union** for notice and paid training.
I would insist on **traceable figures** before a return is signed.
think: I expect a **large cut** to my junior paid hours.
Farah's part-time pay cannot cover our **rent** alone.
do: Join the **staff union** to seek written notice and paid training before cuts.
Take the **required AI walkthrough** only with a written requirement, paid time and supervisor demonstration; retain offered paid files.
Take **posted clerk work** after cuts only with written pay covering rent and food after fares, hours and start.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected wage loss.
S1.quote: I can learn a required screen if someone pays me to do it.
fieldNote: Her junior **data entry and checking** are exposed immediately, long before capable physical robots.
Training requires **written requirements** and paid time; a job move needs posted written terms after bus fares.

steps.text: Join staff union to seek written notice and paid training
Take written-required AI walkthrough on paid time with supervisor demonstration; retain offered paid files
Take posted clerk work after cuts with written rent-and-food pay after fares, hours and start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could enter, check and explain my schedules more cheaply than the firm pays me. Robots around 2031 are later for carrying stock, but my desk will not get those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to press for written severance and notice before junior posts disappear. I would tell the florist I cannot promise a named junior will still enter the slips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my post to end in 2028, and Farah's part-time wage cannot cover the rent and bills alone. Our savings would last weeks, not months; I wake up wondering which bill would come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union for a written notice and severance process and keep every paid file the firm still assigns. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I would use the small reserve for rent and food while applying to actual posted payroll-clerk jobs, taking one only with written wage, hours and a start date that cover rent and bus fare. Payroll is also screen work, so I would treat a real paid post as a bridge rather than a safe new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect the job to go and do not have a long reserve. I am frightened, but I can still ask for terms and look for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children what is happening, but I would not count on their money. If a bill is about to be missed, I would contact the landlord before the due date instead of hiding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before the firm makes a decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep taking the paid shifts offered until the post actually ends or a signed new start date arrives. After dismissal, there is no old wage to keep.

say: I would seek **written severance** through the union.
I would explain that **2028 desk AGI** comes before 2031 robots.
think: I expect my **junior post** to end when AGI handles schedules.
Our **weeks of savings** cannot replace my wage through a long search.
do: Ask the **union** for severance and keep paid files only while offered.
After loss, use the **small reserve** for rent and food during the posted payroll search.
Take a **posted payroll job** only with written rent- and fare-covering wage, hours and start.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about likely job loss and a short reserve.
S2.quote: After dismissal, there is no old wage to keep.
fieldNote: Her thin reserve and few nearby jobs make the **2028 deadline** severe despite a practical search plan.
Payroll remains **screen work** exposed to AGI; she calls a paid opening a bridge and does not assume family money.

steps.text: Ask union for written severance; keep paid files only while offered
After loss use reserve for bills; take posted payroll job with written rent-and-fare-covering wage hours start
Before missed rent contact landlord about payment timing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to look at actual vacancies before the screen work faces AGI in 2031. Robots around 2034 are later for carrying goods, not for entering the florist's tax figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm and union for a paid route into checking customer disputes. I would tell colleagues a certificate is only useful if a real wage follows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect my entry work to shrink, but a few years could let me learn a narrow task while I have pay. I am not a senior adviser, and I cannot spend our rent money on a course to pretend I am one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in the basic accounts-dispute course only if the firm gives a written paid clerk vacancy for it, covers the fee and gives paid study hours; otherwise I would use free union notes while keeping assigned paid returns. Before or after 2031, I would take that posted clerk vacancy only with written wage, hours and start date covering rent and bus fare. If the present post ends first, I would use the small reserve for bills during the search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the likely hour loss, although five years lets me ask for a real paid route. I cannot retire on a promise of retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm offers only a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the free notes and keep the paid filing work still assigned. I would not buy a qualification without a posted wage to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know when you can retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see retirement getting nearer, but I do not know what income it would provide yet. I need written figures before I treat it as an answer to losing work.

say: I would seek a **paid clerk route** through the firm and union.
I would ask for a **posted wage** before buying a certificate.
think: My **entry work** may shrink when AGI reaches the desk in 2031.
I cannot use **rent money** for speculative training.
do: Read **free union notes** while paid; enrol only for a written paid vacancy with funded fee and study hours.
Keep **assigned paid returns** while offered; after loss use the reserve for bills.
Take a **posted dispute clerk job** only with written rent- and fare-covering wage, hours and start.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely hour cuts.
S3.quote: I cannot retire on a promise of retraining.
fieldNote: She keeps the proposed role at **clerk level**; five years does not turn her into a senior adviser.
Enrolment requires a **written paid vacancy**, funded fee and paid hours; free notes and current shifts remain the fallback.

steps.text: Read free notes; enrol only for written paid vacancy with funded fee and paid study hours
Keep paid returns while offered; after loss use reserve for bills
Take posted clerk job with written rent- and fare-covering wage hours start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would put me at 68 when AGI reaches the desk in 2036. Robots around 2039 are later; I cannot assume the filing work survives until I choose to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the employer for a written statement of my retirement income and work options, and ask the union to explain it in plain words. I would tell my grown children only what the figures actually show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope I could retire during that decade, but I do not know whether any income due to me would cover rent and food. With under a month saved now, I cannot simply announce a date and stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a written retirement-income projection and compare it with rent, food and travel before setting a date. I would keep paid florist schedules while the firm offers them; in the first year after 2036, if I still need wages and the post ends, I would use the reserve for bills and seek a posted clerk job only with written wage, hours and start date covering rent and travel. If the projection truly covers essentials, I would make a retirement decision then, not assume it today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the present bills, even with a decade to check the figures. A birthday is not a payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the grown children to support retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our grown children have their own rent and plans. I can ask them to read a confusing letter, not to underwrite a date I have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the projection is too small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep taking paid work while offered and search for an actual posted clerk opening if this one ends. I would not stop because someone said people my age usually do.

say: I would ask for a **written income projection** before naming a retirement date.
I would tell family only what the **figures actually show**.
think: I do not know if retirement income would cover **rent and food**.
Our **thin reserve** means I need wages until the numbers prove otherwise.
do: Request a **written retirement projection**; consider a date only if projected income covers rent, food and travel.
Keep **paid florist schedules** while offered; after loss use reserve for bills if wages remain necessary.
Seek **posted clerk work** after 2036 loss if wages remain necessary, with written rent/travel-covering pay, hours and start.
feel: I feel **anxious** about today's bills and uncertain retirement income.
S4.quote: A birthday is not a payslip.
fieldNote: At 68 in 2036 she may be near retirement, but **no entitlement** or sufficient income is assumed.
The projection governs retirement; if wages remain necessary, she keeps **paid work** while offered and seeks a real vacancy.

steps.text: Request written projection; consider retirement only if income covers rent food travel
Keep paid florist schedules while offered; after loss use reserve if wages needed
Seek posted clerk work after 2036 loss if wages needed, with written rent/travel-pay hours/start

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the job to go before I can build even a month's reserve. Paid notice, severance and a real posted clerk job with rent-covering terms would help; a course only helps if the firm pays for it and there is work afterward.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what my retirement income will actually be. I do not know my retirement income yet, and I will not make our rent depend on a guess.

headlineQuote: I do not know my retirement income yet, and I will not make our rent depend on a guess.
portrait: Dana is a **58-year-old junior accountant** with a bachelor's degree who is still learning florist returns.
Her **low pay**, under-one-month reserve and few nearby firms make even the mild world anxious.
She **never uses AI** and would take only required, written, paid instruction.
She checks **actual retirement income** before stopping work and needs posted paid alternatives if filing ends.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** case could end her junior wage before she builds a reserve.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid notice and severance**, plus a posted rent-covering clerk role and funded training tied to work.
